title: Phygital customer experience and the adoption of immersive technologies in hospitality: an exploratory study with a value co-creation perspective
abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore immersive-technology adoption in hospitality through the Phygital Customer Experience (PH-CX) framework. PH-CX extends existing technology acceptance, service-dominant logic, omnichannel and customer-journey perspectives by emphasizing embodied, co-created and human-centered experience across physical, digital and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated interactions. Design/methodology/approach Using Bayesian Networks, the study examines probabilistic dependencies among perceived usefulness, collaborative value, responsive co-creation attitudes and intention to use immersive technologies. Data was collected from 208 participants exposed to an AI-supported immersive hotel journey scenario. The analysis is exploratory and identifies conditional associations rather than causal effects or latent-variable relationships. Findings Adoption intention was conditionally associated with perceived usefulness, collaborative value and responsiveness to service innovation. The findings suggest that immersive-hospitality engagement involves functional, relational and participatory conditions beyond usefulness alone. However, the item-level results are hypothesis-generating and do not demonstrate PH-CX’s incremental predictive superiority over technology acceptance model (TAM) or service-dominant logic. Research limitations/implications The scenario-based, cross-sectional bayesian network (BN) design cannot model latent constructs, measurement error, mediation or causal effects. Future studies should validate PH-CX dimensions and compare TAM, TAM-plus-service-dominant logic (SDL) and PH-CX models using structural equation modeling, longitudinal designs and holdout-sample prediction. Practical implications Hotels can implement PH-CX through phased AI concierge pilots, cross-platform data integration and guest co-creation mechanisms. Relevant metrics include booking conversion, AI resolution rates, cross-channel engagement, co-creation participation and net promoter score (NPS). Ethical implementation requires transparency, opt-in participation, privacy safeguards, accessibility and human escalation options. Social implications Human-centered phygital hospitality requires safeguards against digital exclusion, surveillance and loss of human warmth. Transparency, agency, equity, privacy and non-digital alternatives are essential for inclusive and trustworthy service innovation. Originality/value The study advances PH-CX as a theory-extending framework linking usefulness, co-creation, embodied experience and ethical safeguards in immersive hospitality. It also proposes experience-design orientation as a future research profile and offers a phased implementation framework for responsible phygital service design.

title: Ziziphus spina-christi leaf extract in schistosomal liver disease: Biomarker gains in hepatectomy model-perioperatively actionable?
abstract: Schistosomiasis is a major neglected tropical disease that leads to periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension, and compromised hepatic reserve. In endemic regions, the disease persists despite anthelmintic therapy, thereby increasing surgical risks. This editorial discusses the study by Alghamdi published in the World Journal of Hepatology , which evaluates the effects of Ziziphus spina-christi leaf extract (ZSCLE) in a hamster model of Schistosoma mansoni-induced fibrosis undergoing 50% partial hepatectomy. The study demonstrated that ZSCLE reduced hepatic egg burden, improved biochemical markers and inflammatory markers, activated cellular injury responses, and increased regeneration indices. Although these preclinical findings indicate potential benefits, they do not yet establish clinical perioperative efficacy due to the absence of definitive outcomes, such as post-hepatectomy liver failure, bleeding/transfusion surrogates, survival, and dynamic reserve testing. The central clinical question remains whether ZSCLE enhances hepatic tolerance and recovery following major surgical stress, possibly through anti-inflammatory/antioxidant signaling or direct antiparasitic activity, beyond improvements in biochemical markers alone. Future development of ethnomedicines should prioritize standardized research methodologies, comprehensive safety evaluations, and investigations incorporating clinically relevant functional endpoints and hard clinical outcomes to ensure both efficacy and safety in clinical settings.

title: Why employee silence persists: unequal capacity to bear the consequences of speaking up
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop capacity to bear voice consequences to explain why employees anticipating comparable repercussions from speaking up may make different communication choices. It examines how unequal protection shapes silence within a voice episode and how experience can alter later choices. Design/methodology/approach The conceptual argument integrates employee voice and silence research with conservation of resources theory, career scholarship and employment relations to develop propositions linking anticipated exposure, available capacity and perceived capacity. Findings The model proposes that anticipated consequence exposure is more strongly associated with silence when perceived capacity is low. Available capacity comprises resources that employees can access and mobilise to absorb, contain or recover from specified losses. Perceived capacity concerns their assessment of that protection. Appraisals may underestimate or exceed the protection available at the decision point. Communication arrangements and experiences of harm or protection may alter exposure, capacity and subsequent choices. Originality/value The contribution specifies how resources become protective through their fit with anticipated consequences. By distinguishing available protection from its appraisal, the model explains why comparable anticipated events can exert unequal behavioural influence across employees. It connects resource inequality with silence through a proposed interaction between exposure and perceived capacity, then examines how that relationship may change across episodes.

title: What drives EU economic growth? Key takeaways in a shifting global economy
journal: Review of Economics and Political Science
abstract: Purpose This study explores the key drivers of economic growth in the EU from 2000 to 2024, focusing on investment, trade openness, government expenditure and R&D. Using panel data from 27 EU countries, the research examines how these variables influence GDP per capita growth, emphasizing the role of human capital, foreign direct investment (FDI) and manufacturing. Design/methodology/approach The study employs the generalized method of moments (GMM) to address endogeneity and obtain robust estimates. The model includes lagged GDP per capita growth, investment, trade openness and government expenditure, along with R&D-related variables such as researchers per million inhabitants and tertiary school enrollment. The analysis also explores variations based on R&D intensity and transition status. Findings Results indicate that trade openness significantly boosts economic growth, with manufacturing growth playing a key role, particularly in higher R&D-intensity countries. Government expenditure and investment appear insignificant, while tertiary enrollment can have negative effects, depending on the context. Originality/value This study provides novel insights into the heterogeneous effects of R&D and human capital on EU economic growth, emphasizing the importance of trade and industrial policies in fostering long-term development.

title: Travel without movement: understanding the impact of immersive technologies on virtual tourism experiences
journal: Consumer Behavior in Tourism and Hospitality
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how immersive digital technologies shape virtual tourism by investigating the mediating role of user engagement in the relationships among digital technology adoption, accessibility, content quality, interactivity and the effectiveness of virtual tourism experiences. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted using a structured online survey of 235 respondents with prior virtual tourism experience, selected through purposive and snowball sampling. Data were analyzed using SPSS and AMOS using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Findings User engagement significantly mediates the relationships between technological attributes and virtual tourism effectiveness. Content quality and digital technology adoption demonstrate strong direct and indirect effects, accessibility and interactivity operate only through engagement, suggesting that experiential immersion depends more on cognitive and emotional engagement than on functional interaction alone. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for platform developers, destination marketers and policymakers on designing immersive, accessible and user-centered virtual tourism environments that enhance engagement and broaden access to tourism experiences. Social implications Virtual tourism can promote more inclusive tourism participation by providing access to destinations for individuals facing physical, financial, or geographical barriers to travel. By complementing physical tourism, immersive digital experiences can broaden cultural exposure and support more equitable access to tourism experiences. Originality/value This study extends virtual tourism literature by integrating technological, psychological and experiential dimensions within a unified framework that explains how user engagement translates technological attributes into effective virtual tourism experiences.

title: The more confident the more digital? A study of the mechanisms of CEO overconfidence on corporate digital transformation
abstract: Purpose This study examines how CEO overconfidence influences corporate digital transformation and explores the cognitive-behavioral mechanisms underlying this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Using a panel dataset of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2024, this study constructs a language-based measure of CEO overconfidence from CEOs' personal social media posts and their directly attributable statements reported in publicly available sources. Two-way fixed-effects models are employed to examine the relationship between CEO overconfidence and corporate digital transformation, supplemented by robustness checks including alternative measures, additional fixed effects, instrumental variable analyses and Heckman two-stage analysis. Findings The results show that CEO overconfidence is positively associated with firms' digital transformation. This effect operates primarily through entrepreneurial orientation and strategic risk-taking, with the two mechanisms forming a sequential mediating relationship. Furthermore, the positive effect of CEO overconfidence on digital transformation is strengthened when CEOs possess an IT background and greater CEO power, as well as when firms have higher levels of resource slack and operate in regions with higher levels of market development, but is weakened in state-owned enterprises. Originality/value This study advances upper echelons theory by developing a commitment-based account of how CEO overconfidence shapes strategic change under uncertainty and by specifying a cognition–posture–action process through which executive cognition is translated into firm-level digital transformation. Methodologically, it introduces a language-based measure of CEO overconfidence derived from CEOs' linguistic expressions, offering an alternative approach to capturing executive cognition beyond traditional financial proxies.

title: The Influence of the Non-Arabic Tongue on Qur'anic Recitation: A Contrastive Phonetic Study of Samples from Visiting Students in the Qur'an Circles of the Sacred Mosque in Makkah
journal: AL-Lisan International Journal for Linguistic & Literary Studies
abstract: Abstract: This research examines the impact of the mother tongue on the Quranic recitation of non-Arabic speakers, based on observations recorded by the researcher while teaching in the study circles of the Grand Mosque (Al-Masjid Al-Haram) during Rajab 1447 AH. The study observed twenty-five visiting students reciting according to the narration of Ḥafṣ ‘an ‘Āṣim: ten from West Africa and fifteen from Southeast Asia. Utilizing a descriptive-analytical approach alongside contrastive analysis, the study evaluated deviations using the criteria of manifest (al-laḥn al-jalī) and hidden (al-laḥn al-khafiyy) errors established by tajwīd scholars. The findings indicate that shared deviations between the two groups concentrate on the letters ḥā' (ح), ‘ayn (ع), and emphasized (muṭbaqah) sounds. The most prominent difference between the groups lies in the degree of deviation: complete substitution predominated among the African students, whereas approximation predominated among the Asian students—a difference the research attributes to the level of emphasis placed on tajwīd instruction. Furthermore, the study revealed causes of deviation that cannot be predicted solely by comparing the phonologies of the two languages, such as over-correction, adjacency effects (assimilation/coarticulation), and syllable constraints. It concludes with remedial exercises based on minimal pairs derived from Quranic vocabulary. Keywords: Non-Arabic tongue (Al-Lisān Al-‘Ajamī), Quranic performance, manifest and hidden errors (al-laḥn al-jalī and al-khafiyy), contrastive analysis, linguistic interference, Grand Mosque study circles.

title: Behavioral intention to use FinTech lending based on a holistic theory – Does lifestyle of hedonic consumption matter?
journal: Journal of Economic and Administrative Sciences
abstract: Purpose This study empirically tests the effects of effort expectancy (EE), performance expectancy (PE), social influence (SI), facilitating conditions (FC), attitude, subjective norm (SN), perceived behavioral control (PBC), and lifestyle of hedonic consumption (LOHC) on behavioral intention to use FinTech lending (BIUFL) and actual usage of FinTech lending (AUFL). Design/methodology/approach This study utilized convenience sampling to select 350 university students from Indonesia. Data were collected using an online questionnaire. Data were analyzed using variance-based structural equation modeling with WarpPLS. Findings Our study found that PE, attitude, PBC, and LOHC were essential factors in BIUFL. We report that the EE, SI, FC, and SN do not affect BIUFL. Finally, BIUFL was found to positively influence AUFL. Practical implications Regulators enhance supervision by issuing regulations that set strict requirements for Gen Z to access FinTech lending, particularly regarding prospective customers' ability to repay credit, and add parental consent as an additional requirement for Gen Z. Originality/value We employ a holistic research model that combines the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT), theory of planned behavior (TPB), and LOHC to explain students' BIUFL.
